source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, banana cultivation techniques manual, 2019, section V.2.4 (fruit fly)
text:
The fruit fly cited here, Dacus dorsalis (Oriental fruit fly, now generally classified as Bactrocera dorsalis), attacks a range of fruit crops including guava, mango, and banana, and is most active in the cooler parts of the day (morning and evening). The adult is a small (roughly 0.7cm), brown fly with yellowish markings and clear, patterned wings. Females pierce the fruit skin to lay eggs inside; eggs hatch in about 8-12 days, and the resulting larvae feed inside the flesh, causing internal rot and often premature fruit drop. A single fruit can host large numbers of larvae, and a female fly can lay well over a thousand eggs across her roughly 1-3 month lifespan, so populations can build up quickly where fallen or overripe fruit is left in the field.

Because infestation often isn't visible from the outside until the fruit is already rotting, fruit fly damage is a particular concern for growers aiming to sell higher-value or export-grade fruit, since infested fruit can be rejected even if damage is only discovered after harvest.

Prevention and control: collect and destroy fallen or infested fruit promptly rather than leaving it in the field; bag developing fruit with paper or plastic to physically prevent females from laying eggs; hang bait traps containing an attractant (methyl eugenol lures specifically attract male flies) combined with insecticide to reduce the breeding population; and where needed, apply Malathion 83% EC insecticide following label directions.
